Reviewer Expertise:

Sport and nutrition

I confirm that I have read this submission and believe that I have an appropriate level of expertise to confirm that it is of an acceptable scientific standard, however I have significant reservations, as outlined above.

Thanks to the editor for the invitation, some improvement suggestions are as follows:

The core connotation and adaptation logic of frugal innovation have not been clearly explained, resulting in a lack of convincing "why it applies to local government smart city business models". The paper only mentions "doing more with less resources" and does not distinguish its essential differences from traditional low-cost models and lean models, nor does it explain its unique advantages in the public sector scenario (such as adapting to fiscal constraints and emphasizing people's livelihood orientation).

The paper uses "performance" and "inclusiveness" as auxiliary keywords, but does not include the core concern "financial sustainability" into the core search combination, and does not consider synonymous substitutions (for example,"local government","municipal government" and "city council" need to be fully covered, and "cost-effective innovation" can be added as a synonymous expression of frugality and innovation). It is recommended to reconstruct the keyword combination with "(smart city) AND (business model OR financial sustainability) AND (local authority OR municipality OR local government) AND (frugal innovation OR cost-effective innovation)" as the core, and at the same time eliminate auxiliary keywords that are weak related to the research topic to avoid interference from irrelevant literature and improve screening accuracy.

From 33,273 initial documents to 300 "Smart City Business Model" documents to 17 "Local Government-Related" documents, the exclusion criteria at each step only mentioned "irrelevant" in general and did not clearly state the specific basis for "irrelevant"., and the specific reasons for the exclusion of the 13 documents were not marked one by one. It is recommended to supplement the complete PRISMA flow chart, detailing the number of screening and exclusion criteria at each step (such as inconsistent topics, non-local governments, and no business model discussion), and explain the selection basis for the four included core documents to ensure that the study is repeatable.

The paper only lists 10 business models such as PPP and subscription, and does not analyze the applicable conditions of each model in the smart city scenario (such as what types of smart city projects the PPP model is suitable for and what prerequisites are required), financial sustainability performance (such as investment return cycle, risk sharing mechanism), nor does it discuss obstacles to the implementation of the model in conjunction with the administrative attributes and fiscal constraints of local governments. It is recommended to increase comparative analysis of business models, build an evaluation framework from four dimensions: "capital needs, operation difficulty, public welfare adaptability, and financial sustainability", and combine cases in existing literature (such as the effectiveness of subscription system for smart parking in a city, Failure lessons from a regional PPP model) to clarify the advantages and disadvantages of different models and application scenarios.

The three-element framework of "user-business-technology" proposed in the paper only stays at the conceptual level and does not explain the specific implementation path of frugal innovation under each element (for example,"minimum resources" in the technical elements refer to simplifying the technical architecture and reusing existing facilities, or adopting open source technology), nor does it define the interaction between various elements. It is recommended to refine the dimensions of the framework, for example, add the sub-dimensions of "revenue source, cost control, risk sharing" to the "commercial elements", and clarify specific directions such as "technology selection, facility reuse, and operation and maintenance simplification" in the "technical elements", and combine 1-2 virtual cases (such as frugal and innovative design of local government smart government services) to demonstrate the application logic of the framework.

The paper focuses on Malaysia's 150 local councils, but does not analyze their unique fiscal structure (such as tax dependence, transfer payment ratio), the financing difficulties of existing smart city projects (such as whether any projects have stalled due to funding shortages), and policy environment constraints (such as regulatory barriers to public-private partnerships), resulting in a lack of realistic adaptability of research conclusions.

The paper does not discuss why there is a gap in research on the relationship between frugal innovation and smart city business models. Is it due to lack of academic understanding, lack of practical cases, or is it limited in research methods? Nor has it learned from the application experience of frugal innovation in other public service fields (such as education and medical care) to provide ideas for filling the gap.

Reviewer Expertise:

pedagogy, communication

I confirm that I have read this submission and believe that I have an appropriate level of expertise to confirm that it is of an acceptable scientific standard, however I have significant reservations, as outlined above.

Drawing on a systematic search of the extensive peer-reviewed literature, the article demonstrates that the applicability of a ‘frugal innovation’ business model has not attracted academic attention in relation to the smart city. By extension, it encourages researchers to explore this topic, in order to inform more sustainable modes of funding smart city programmes.

The basic finding about the gap in the literature is fairly straightforward, but clearly evidenced. For the article to be published, however, a rather more substantial framing of the research aims is required, along with a more generative set of conclusions.

A key reservation for me, as a reader not previously familiar with the idea of frugal innovation, is that I am left feeling unpersuaded about the reasons why this particular business model is worthy of future attention. I am sure there are all manner of other topics – and business models - which are not covered in the smart city literature – but that absence does not in itself justify further research. Certainly, if it can be shown that funding models are currently inadequate, then there would be good reason to explore new approaches, and especially those which have proven successful in somehow related governance contexts. As things stand, the authors do mention that frugal innovation has been applied to engineering and industrial design, but do not explain why it would therefore be “worth investigating” in relation to the smart city. If the smart city was largely a question of engineering or industrial design, then the relevance of frugal innovation would perhaps be self-evident. But can private sector business models be applied so easily to local government contexts? The article claims that “literature and evidence in frugal innovation prove that it can be a game-changer for a sustainable business model” (p.10), but in what ways in particular? Why specifically might this be relevant to local authorities?

Further explaining the need for research into this topic (beyond the existence of a research gap) seems vital to me if the article is to be indexed. A starting point would be to provide further insight into what frugal innovation involves – beyond the buzzwords flagged up in Figure 3. Please tell us more about how this differs from other approaches, and what others might have said about its potential applications. Are there any other fields of local authority activity, for example, where it has been applied? Which of its basic principles seem clearly relevant to smart city development? In what ways specifically does it depart from a ‘conventional business model’? (Is there only one conventional/traditional business model in any case?) Is it perhaps a new idea which has spread rapidly across lots of different fields?

Ideally, I would also like to see some concrete evidence that current funding models are not sustainable. I don’t have reason to doubt this, and the fact that it came up as a significant issue at the 2018 conference mentioned on p.3 is a good start. ‘Smart city’ programmes usually consist of specific projects in reality (which may in reality be rather small-scale) – but would it be possible to provide examples of envisioned projects in Malaysia which will probably not happen due to funding obstacles? Any examples from elsewhere of grand visions being cut down to scale, or specific initiatives being dropped for financial reasons?

For the article to be published, I would also like to see the conclusions fleshed out a little. Drawing on an earlier discussion of the reasons why frugal innovation might be relevant (as proposed above), what particular research questions should researchers be asking? What might the limitations of frugal innovation be? What more theoretical interventions might be enabled by such research? What kinds of methods do you have in mind?

I have a few more specific comments for the authors to address:

Abstract: the three sentences from “Local authorities” to “smart city initiatives” could easily be condensed into one.

P3: “Traditionally, cities are funded by government, for example, through tax collection”. This point could be much sharper. Surely, city services etc. are typically provided through tax collection – but what do you mean by “cities”? Isn’t much of the city funded by private investment? And what do you mean by ‘traditionally’? For decades, a wide array of governance and funding models have been at play in all sorts of cities, involving the private sector and all sorts of other stakeholders.

The three objectives simply repeat the three research questions. I’m not sure in any case that the third objective could be met from the present study (and it hasn’t been). I suggest rephrasing the third one as more of an overall research aim - for example: "Overall, the article aims to encourage researchers to explore the potential relevance and limitations of the frugal innovation business model to the funding of smart city projects in local authority areas”.

Methods: the second and third paragraphs of the “Ethics” subsection are not related to ethics. Wouldn’t it be better to place the ethics point at the end of the methods section (or have it as a footnote)?

Methods: clarify key point: were you searching on keywords appearing in the front matter of the articles, or looking for their appearance in the main text of the articles? (I’m guessing the latter.)

Methods: the definition of ‘quality’ is a little odd. Are all published journal articles of good quality? If peer review is the criterion, are all conference papers properly peer reviewed?  “Journal/conference papers and research articles” is fuzzy – are research articles not papers? I think it would be better simply to specify that the evidence base consisted of articles and conference papers listed by the online databases shown on page 5.

Figure 2 doesn’t add value - it just repeats what has appeared in the text. Couldn’t this be deleted?

Page 7: “When further analysed…” It would be good to reword the end of this sentence for clarity – is the point that they contain no substantial discussion of business models, even though these words appear in the text?

Page 7 “A good business model would increase a smart city’s chance of success”. This does not seem like a useful analytical point. Isn’t it self-evident?

Page 8 (point 2): this just lists out what appears in Table 2. Surely, what is needed here is discussion and analysis of some sort.

Finally, I haven’t gone through closely looking for typos, but I happened to notice the following, in case it’s helpful:

Abstract: “prosperous living conditions initiatives” could be more elegantly worded. Maybe “quality of life initiatives”?

Abstract: “data is” should really be “data are”.

Abstract: “The data is tabulated for clear expression of knowledge gaps” – not sure what you mean. Could you just delete this? (Does it just mean that some findings have been presented as tables?)

Abstract: delete comma after “further” in the final sentence.

Abstract and first para: put single speech marks around ‘frugal innovation’ the first time it appears, since it is a technical term.

Intro second para: “the paper concludes” (not concluded).

Smart City Phenomenon: delete comma after “world”.  “Tipped” should also be rephrased – maybe just “exceeded”.

Smart City Phenomenon: “in regards that” – rephrase eg “with regards to the need for…”

P4: “systematic” rather than “systemic”.

P7: delete comma after “initiatives”.

I confirm that I have read this submission and believe that I have an appropriate level of expertise to confirm that it is of an acceptable scientific standard, however I have significant reservations, as outlined above.

Dear Authors,

There are some interesting proposals in your manuscript as well as some relevant shortcomings, please take a look at my comments below and - first and foremost - take care of proposing implications.

Introduction:

In the very first lines you refer to smart (and sustainable) city initiatives but you recall digital city services, please be aware of the difference and note it it at the beginning. I would suggest you to see what scholars mention about the comparison of these topics. You can refer to several publications, I can mention few as examples: Hollands, R. G (2008) 
                1, Tregua, M., D’Auria, A., & Bifulco, F.

(2014)
                2, and Ishida, T. (2017).
                3

You recalled the notion of smart city, I'd do that with a definition and a quote from one of the most important works in this domain, e.g., Giffinger, R. (2015),
                4 or Fernandez-Anez, V., Fernández-Güell, J. M., & Giffinger, R. (2018).
                5

Finally, I agree with your justification of the reason to perform this study, but since you deal with business models and several big firms have proposed their solutions for smart cities, I would wrap up the introduction by recalling a model or two proposed by big companies such as IBM, Microsoft, Cisco, and so on.

Please complete the introduction with a description of the structure of the chapter.

Method

This section is well written and reliable; anyway, there are two missing elements:

a) I would start from previous reviews, if any, to justify the reason for your study.

b) I would describe how you avoided subjectivity in your selection of extant literature.

Results:

Referring to table 2 is not enough to justify/describe your two research gaps. Please debate it some more. Table 2 simply reports the evidence you picked up, while it is needed to clearly state why what you reported led you to highlight a research gap.

Moreover, I wonder why this section is called results, since there are no 'real' results. This section is not actually hosting results, but

it is a description of the process you carried out.

Discussion:

I agree with your consideration on smart cities, as per the text in the first 5 lines. This consideration would have worked even better with a definition of smart city in the first section of this manuscript.

Sub-section 2 of the Discussion:

This view is limited, since big companies have their business model for smart cities. Thus, either you should explicitly consider them too, or highlight if these models are recalled by scholars in the contributions you analysed. Considering big companies would lead you to observe how business models for smart cities were set. Moreover, local agencies very often involve big companies in running smart cities projects and they cooperate in defining a business model suitable for a specific area. This is also relevant in considering 'how' and 'why' a big company gets involved in such projects.

Conclusions:

I am very surprised by the lack of implications. I agree with some of your considerations, but such a manuscript would have a very limited usefulness with nor theoretical neither practical implications and appears as an opinion paper instead of being a research paper.

The study has fulfilled the aims, i.e. to estimate the prevalence values of IAD in different Spanish communities from 2011 to 2016; however, I would have appreciated some discussion about the reasons why the prevalence of IAD in Spain is low.

I confirm that I have read this submission and believe that I have an appropriate level of expertise to state that I do not consider it to be of an acceptable scientific standard, for reasons outlined above.

In the current paper, the authors proposed to assess the effectiveness of the acute ingestion of L-arginine on muscle strength and other related to muscle performance. I found some serious limitations in the current version of the paper.

Major comments:

How can we trust the conclusions of a meta-analysis based on 3 studies and 30 subjects? This should be clear in the discussion. I noticed that the authors included this as a limitation, but there is no discussion about how serious this limitation is.

Authors should be able to justify grouping distinct muscle groups (i.e., upper and lower body) and variables in only one measure to conduct this meta-analysis.

Please be aware that heterogeneity I2 statistics is based on Cochran’s Q, which is hugely influenced by the number of studies. If the number of studies is too low (e.g. n=3), I2 will probably be low. Therefore, I am not sure if the result of this statistic can be trusted in the current paper.

Please provide a detailed search strategy for each database so readers can properly reproduce your search if needed.

Please describe the online tools or software used during the screening of the 1075 references.

Please include information about the model used for meta-analysis (e.g., fixed effect or random effects). In the methods, I found this only in the legend of figure 5. Also, I was not able to find information about what type of meta-analysis was conducted, is this a two-level or a three-level meta-analysis?

In the legend of figure 5, the authors stated that the fixed effect model was used. How can we use a fixed-effect model when study populations, doses, exercises, testing, and outcomes are not identical between studies? There are some relevant differences when comparing the 3 studies.

The authors stated using RoB2 tool to conduct RoB analysis (
                https://sites.google.com/site/riskofbiastool/welcome/rob-2-0-tool/current-version-of-rob-2?authuser=0). However, the domains and final reported RoB data do not match RoB2, but do match the original Cochrane RoB analysis (
                https://www.bmj.com/content/343/bmj.d5928)
                1. Please revise.

Please describe the software used to generate RoB figures.

It is not clear why the authors would use the "Assessment of Multiple Systematic Reviews (AMSTAR2)" in the current paper, since this is a tool to assess the quality of systematic reviews, not RCT (
                https://www.bmj.com/content/358/bmj.j4008)
                2. This tool is usually applied in umbrella reviews or reviews of systematic reviews. Please clarify why you are using this tool here. Also, there is no clear mention regarding the results of such analysis in the paper.

The authors state that "however, there was still good precision" in the quality of evidence analysis. What were the criteria for that? It is important to include in the methods what was considered a small, moderate, and big effect size or what would be considered as a relevant change.

A big part of the discussion does not fit the scope of the meta-analysis. The authors spent a lot of time citing and describing the use of L-arginine for other applications or other modalities of exercise.

General comments:

The version of figure 5 available to me does not look good for publication.

I found some minor punctuation and inconsistent use of "L-arg" in the text.

Overall, the authors should consider writing a paper including the systematic review and a narrative/scope review describing the 3 papers, but not a meta-analysis if we only have 3 studies on the topic.

This manuscript describes the similarity between outcomes used to evaluate health technologies and the outcomes included in Core Outcomes Sets (COS). Attempts to evaluate the effects of health technologies - termed health technology assessments (HTAs) - were identified through the International Network of Agencies for Health Technology Assessments (INHATA) and the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) website. 90% of identified HTAs were systematic reviews and the remainder were trials. Ten COS that were developed for common diseases in collaboration with patients, and published between 2015 and 2019 were identified from the COMET database. Basic descriptive statistics were used to describe the similarity between outcomes in HTAs and each COS, to compare the populations and interventions targeted by COS and HTAs, and to describe changes in the level of similarity between COS and HTAs over time. The study's primary limitation, which the authors acknowledge, is that the vast majority of HTAs eligible for inclusion in the study did not have functional hyperlinks in INHATA, and it is unclear to what extent the included studies are representative of the entire target population of HTAs. Put another way, the external validity of the HTAs described is unknown.

My primary recommendation regards how the study's results have been interpreted. Conclusions in both the abstract and body of the manuscript address awareness, acceptance, and implementation of COS by the people designing HTAs. However, the temporal relationship between the publication of COS and the design of HTAs included in this study is not straightforward. Fully 60% of included HTAs were published before 2015 (and possibly designed years before publication), while the 10 COS were published between in 2015 and later. In Figure 2, there does not appear to be a temporal trend between 2009 and 2020 in the degree of similarity between COS and HTA outcomes. Thus, another interpretation of these results is that COS developers consistently include 40 - 70% of the outcomes assessed by HTAs when developing their COS and this does not appear to be changing. I recommend performing a sub-group analysis of HTAs developed after the publication of relevant COS to address this chicken-and-egg problem. The results of such an analysis may permit stronger and more substantiated inferences about the awareness, acceptance, and implementation of COS.
